titleStmt.title: Best-Case Analysis for Improving the Worst-Case Schedulability Test for Distributed Hard Real-Time Systems

analytic.title: Best-Case Analysis for Improving the Worst-Case Schedulability Test for Distributed Hard Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This work has been supported in part by the Comisión Interministerial de Ciencia y Tecnología of the Spanish Government, under Grant TAP97-892

In this paper we present an improvement of the schedulability analysis technique for distributed hard realtime systems that allows us to increase the maximum schedulable resource utilization. Since the improvement affects only the analysis technique, there is no additional implementation cost for the application itself. The improvement in the analysis consists of calculating a lower bound for the best-case response time of tasks and messages, in order to reduce the estimated jitter in the activation of subsequent tasks and messages. This reduction of jitter implies reduced worst-case bounds for the response times, and thus allows us to increase the maximum schedulable utilization. The paper explores two different ways to calculate a lower bound on the best-case execution times. The paper also shows the results of simulations that we have carried out, in which we found that we could increase the maximum schedulable limit of the different resources by approximately 5% more utilization.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Real-time systems have undergone a notable evolution in the last few years, both in number and variety of applications (every day there are more systems that incorporate time as a fundamental factor in their function), and in complexity (there are more and greater necessities arising, and they require the development of more complex systems). A clear result of this evolution is found in distributed real-time systems, which have an increasing importance in today's control systems, since low-cost networking facilities allow the interconnection of multiple devices and their controllers into a single large system.

The typical architecture in a distributed real-time control system consists of several processor nodes interconnected through one or more interconnection networks. The system's software is composed of concurrent tasks that are often statically allocated to processing nodes because the effects of dynamic node allocation are very difficult to predict for hard real-time systems. Each task may exchange messages with other tasks in the same node or in different nodes. Messages exchanged among tasks in different nodes are also statically allocated to a particular network. Tasks allocated in the same node may also share data or resources via the usual synchronization mechanisms used in shared memory systems. Each task in the system is activated by the arrival of one or more triggering events that may be generated by the external environment, a timer, or by the arrival of a message from another task. Many of these events have an associated timing requirement, such as an end-to-end deadline which is the maximum response time allowed from the arrival of an event to the final completion of its response. During the execution of the response to this event, several tasks may need to be executed in one or more nodes, and several messages exchanged in the network. Other timing requirements may also be imposed on individual actions.

One analysis technique used to assess the schedulability of the real-time system is called Rate Monotonic Analysis (RMA), which is a mathematical technique applicable to systems in which tasks are scheduled by fixed priority [7][6] [5]. The RMA techniques can also be applied to distributed systems [9] [14] by modeling each network as if it were a processor, and each message as if it were a task. The schedulability analysis techniques developed for distributed real-time systems have permitted the solution to some of the problems involving these systems, such as: the optimization of the scheduling and allocation of tasks to processors and messages to networks [13], the optimization of the priority assignment to tasks and messages [1], and the extension of the schedulability analysis techniques to handle complex synchronization patterns among the responses to different event sequences in distributed systems [3][4].

Sun and Liu showed in a recent paper [11] that the algorithm developed by Tindell and Clark for the analysis of this kind of system was incomplete because it did not test all the possible cases. We proved in [8] that the algorithm is valid as it was stated and that it effectively obtains an upper bound for the worst-case response times to external events in distributed systems, because the longest response always occurs within the cases that are currently tested by this algorithm. In addition, in that paper we extended the analysis technique to obtain an upper bound for the local response times of particular actions in a response to an event, thus allowing the definition and verification of local deadlines for elementary actions in distributed systems.

The RMA technique for the general worst-case analysis of a distributed system only obtains an upper bound for the worst-case response times, and thus the exact calculation of the response times is still an open issue. This paper presents a contribution to reducing the pessimism of the RMA schedulability analysis, by reducing the estimation of jitter in the activation times of tasks and messages. Jitter in the activation of a task whose execution is triggered by the arrival of a message is the difference between the worst-case and the best-case response times of the triggering message. Until now, the best case had been considered arbitrarily small, and thus jitter had been considered equal to the estimated worst-case response time. By calculating the best-case response time, we can reduce jitter, and thus enhance the analysis. Of course, it is always possible to reduce the effects of jitter completely, by using an appropriate scheduling algorithm such as the sporadic server [2] or the release guard protocol [10]. However, this kind of scheduling algorithm is not always available, and for many applications the cost is greatly reduced if the system is schedulable by just using a conventional fixed priority scheduler. The work presented in this paper is intended to improve the schedulability limits for this kind of applications.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we give a quick review of the real-time system model and the current analysis technique. Section 3 shows two different methods to calculate a lower bound for the best-case response times of tasks and messages: a trivial method, and an iterative method. Section 4 shows the results of simulations that we have carried out to determine the improvement in the schedulability of the real-time system. Finally, in Section 5 we give our conclusions.

div.head: System Model and Worst-Case Analysis Technique
div.p: The problem of scheduling and analyzing the timing response of concurrent programs executing in the processor resources is quite well defined. We shall assume a preemptive scheduling based on fixed priorities, in order to be able to use RMA for the analysis of the worst-case timing behavior. The scheduling and analysis of the worstcase timing response in the communication resources are also well established. The majority of the standard communication networks do not adapt well to real-time communications, and do not support priority-based scheduling of messages. However, there are some standard communication networks that can be used to carry out hard real-time communications, such as point-to-point lines or the CAN bus. The analysis of the message traffic in these communication resources is carried out using the same RMA techniques as with the processor resources. Thus, we will treat the messages in the communication resources in the same way as the tasks in the processor resources, except for a small blocking term that must be taken into account because the messages are composed of sequences of packets, each of which is indivisible and non preemptive.

We define a linear model of an event-driven distributed system [3][4] in which there is a set of external events sequences (generated by external devices, timers, etc.) which activate tasks that are distributed in different processors. These tasks may in turn generate internal events which activate other tasks on the same processor, or activate messages that are sent through a communications network. The arrival of a message to its destination represents an internal event that may activate one or more tasks. We assume that all the sequences of external events arriving at the system are known in advance, and that the rates at which the events with hard real-time requirements arrive are also known; otherwise, it would be impossible to guarantee the schedulability of the system at compilation time.

Each external event arriving at the system generates a response in the form of a sequence of actions. Each action is activated by the internal events generated by the previous actions. An action may be a task (or a part of a task) executed in a particular processor, or a message sent through a communications network. Usually, the first action of a response is a task. For convenience, we will number actions that are consecutive in the response, with consecutive numbers. We will call e i the external event that activates action a i , and e j-1,j the internal event that activates action a j and was generated by action a j-1 . In the linear model of the distributed system, actions can only be activated from a single event (internal or external), and can only generate one internal event that may, in turn, activate another single action in the same or in a different resource (processor or network).

There are different kinds of timing requirements that a j a 1 a 2 a 3 a j Figure Figure 1 1. Linear model of an event-driven distributed system may be imposed on the actions of the response to an external event. We will call global deadline of a particular action the maximum interval of time that may elapse between the arrival of the external event and the finalization of that action (as opposed to a local deadline, which is measured relative to the arrival of the internal event). The global deadline of the last action in a response will be called the end-to-end deadline. We will call D i the global deadline of action a i , d i the local deadline of that action, and ED k the end-to-end deadline for action a k (which should be the last action in the response sequence).

According to this definition of the linear model for distributed systems, Figure 1 shows the scheme of a linear action that is triggered by an input event and can only generate one output event. The response to the external event sequence is composed of a chain of such linear actions. The period of the external event is inherited by the linear action and also by the output event that it may generate. In Figure 1 we also show an example of a response to an external event which is composed of three linear actions (two tasks and a message). The last action in the response (normally a task) is a special case of a linear action in which the output event is not generated.

The analysis of each resource in the distributed system can be carried out using the normal RMA techniques, but taking into account the effects of jitter or deferred activation. The solution to this problem was proposed by Tindell and Clark [14] and consists of repeating the worstcase analysis iteratively (calculation of worst-case response times and jitter for all the system's resources) starting with jitter values equal to zero. The monotonic dependency of the response time with respect to jitter makes the analysis converge to a stable solution. As a result of the analysis the worst-case global responses are obtained and, from them, it can be proved that the schedulability requirements imposed on the distributed system are met. The system is schedulable when the worst-case global response times of each of the actions are less than or equal to their respective deadlines.

In a similar way as with the definitions of the deadlines, we define R i , the worst-case global response time of action a i , as the time taken from the activation of the external event until the completion of a i in the worst case. The worst case is originated after a critical instant [12]. For the calculation of the worst-case global responses we apply RMA theory to each resource separately; for action a i it is calculated from the following iterative equation [6][12]:

div.head: Best-case Analysis
div.p: Until now we have assumed that the execution time of a task or the length of a message can be arbitrarily small. This would imply that under a best-case scenario, tasks or messages would not be preempted by higher priority tasks, and thus the best-case response time could be arbitrarily small. This assumption is correct from the standpoint that it allows us to obtain a valid upper bound for the jitter term of each task or message, and by applying algorithm WCRT, a valid upper bound for the worst-case response times of tasks and messages. However, it is well known that in many systems the execution times of tasks of the length of messages (and thus their transmission times) are not null even in the best case. If the best-case execution and transmission times can be obtained (or a lower bound for them), it should be possible to decrease the amount of estimated jitter, and thus enhance the worst-case response times of lower priority tasks or messages.

We will define C i b as the estimated lower bound on the best-case execution time of action a i ; thus, each action is characterized by its worst and best-case execution times. If the execution time is deterministic, both times will be the same, but in most cases they will be different. Our problem now is how to calculate the best-case response time for each action a i , or at least a lower bound on the best-case response time, R i b . This value will then be used to obtain the jitter term, J i , of each action a i , as the difference between the worst and best-case estimations for the response time of the preceding action,
div.formula: J i =R i-1 -R i b -1 .

div.p: We can see that the right-hand term in Equation ( 6) is constant, and thus, as the iterative WCRT algorithm makes progress, the jitter terms will have the same tendency as the worst-case response times, R i . In the original algorithm the monotonicity of the worst-case execution times (which can only get larger with each iteration) guaranteed the convergence of the WCRT algorithm if a schedulable solution existed. Consequently, the same monotonic behavior is guaranteed for the algorithm with the new way of calculating the jitter terms, and thus it converges to a solution, if one exists.

div.head: Iterative Best-case Estimation
div.p: As we will see in Section 4, the trivial best-case estimation achieves good results in improving the worstcase schedulability analysis. However, it is easy to notice that a higher lower bound for the best case can be obtained by taking into account preemption from higher priority tasks which, even for the best case, may occur. Figure 2 illustrates this preemption effect with an example. The system has two processors and three different event sequences, e 1 , e 2 , and e 4 , which trigger the execution of three responses. The tasks and the timing parameters of each task and event are show in Figure 2.a. In order to simplify the example, we have assumed that the transmission time for messages between the two processors is negligible, and thus we have not considered the effects of the communications network. According to our model, we assume that the three event sequences are purely periodic, with no jitter. This implies that only task τ 3 has jitter in its activation time, because it is the only task activated by the execution of another task. div.p: Execution of a j The example above has shown that the trivial bestcase response time calculation is too unrealistic, because it does not take into account the effects of preemption by higher priority tasks. We need to find ways to include this preemption effect into the analysis, similar to how it is included in the worst-case analysis. Obviously, the critical instant that is used as a starting point for the worst-case analysis cannot be used here, and thus we need to find a best-case scenario under which we can develop a response time analysis. One possible approach that allows us to obtain a lower bound on the best-case response time is represented by the following lemma.

Lemma 1: Given two actions a i and a j in the same resource, a i having lower priority, the smallest contribution of a j to the response time of a i due to preemption occurs when a j is phased such that no work of a j is pending when a i is activated and, in addition, all the following activations of a j occur at the latest possible time, within its timing constraints.

Proof: First let us suppose that a i is activated during the execution of an instance or job of a j . If we now move the activation time of a i further up in time until the end of the execution of the pending job or jobs of a i , we can only achieve a better response time, because execution of a i and of all the possible successive preemptions by a j will still occur at exactly the same time, and the response time will be counted from a starting point that is later. Now, let us think of the activations of a j that occur after a i has been activated, and that influence the response time of that job of a i . By moving those activations as further up in time as possible, we can only increase the chance of a i finishing earlier, because it has more time to execute. Thus, the lemma follows.

Using Lemma 1, we can extend its results to generate a scenario for obtaining a lower bound on the best-case response time of action a i under the presence of multiple higher priority tasks. The scenario consists of assuming the situation of Lemma 1 for all higher priority tasks, as if they were independent and had not had any interaction or preemption effect among them prior to the activation of a i . Of course it may not be possible to create this scenario in practice, because it is necessary that at the activation of a i all higher priority tasks have just completed execution of their previously pending jobs, simultaneously!. However, although this is a virtually impossible situation, it allows us to obtain a lower bound of the best-case response time of a i , which in reality can only be worse.

In order to build our best-case analysis equations for a i , we will now obtain the activation times of each job of all the higher priority actions involved, which will be phased under the conditions of Lemma 1. Without loss of generality, we will assume the origin of time t=0 at the activation of a i . For each higher priority action, a j , this is also the time of finalization of the last job of that action that was activated before t=0. Let us call t j0 the arrival time of the external event that triggered the response to which a j belongs, for the job that finishes at t=0 (see Figure 3.a).

In our best-case scenario we need to make t j0 the latest possible, because in this way we also make the subsequent jobs of a j occur at the latest possible time (since the external event is periodic). To make t j0 the latest possible, a j would have encountered its best-case response time, and thus t j0 =-R j b . Let us now focus on t j1 , the activation time of the first job of a j after t=0. Taking into account the conditions of Lemma 1, we have to pick the latest possible time for t j1 , which will occur when a j-1 , the action preceding and triggering a j , encounters its worst-case response time. Thus, t j1 shall be equal to T j +R j-1 -R j b , as shown in Figure 3.a. Lastly the following activations of a j will also encounter their worst-case activations, and will therefore occur periodically, with a period of T j , after time t j1 . div.p: We can see in equation ( 15) that the best-case analysis requires knowledge of worst and best-case response times of the different actions. A similar situation happened in the worst-case analysis, where knowledge of the worst-case response times themselves was needed in order to make the analysis. In this latter case, the situation was solved by applying the worst-case analysis iteratively, using for each iteration the results of the previous iteration. The monotonicity of the response times in these iterations -the response times of the next iteration could only get worse if the response times were increased in the current iteration-guaranteed the convergence of the WCRT algorithm if a schedulable solution existed. In order to make sure that algorithm BWCRT converges, we need to check whether the worst-case response times remains monotonic with respect to changes in both the worst and best-case response times of previous iterations. We can see in equation ( 15) that when the worst-case response times increase, the best-case response times get smaller. Also when the best-case response times decrease, the best-case response times obtained in the next iteration also decrease. Finally, as the best-case response times decrease, the jitter terms increase, and thus the worst-case response times also increase. This would confirm the monotonicity of algorithm BWCRT as long as the initial value used for the calculation of the best-case response times is larger than all subsequent values that are obtained through the different iterations.

As we can see in equation (15), it is necessary to find an initial value for each term R j b . In this way, we assure a correct initial value to calculate the best-case response times, and to guarantee the convergence of the algorithm if a solution exists.

div.head: Simulation Results
div.p: This section shows the simulation results carried out by using the two best-case analysis techniques shown in Section 3. The purpose is to find out the improvement in the schedulability of the distributed system. In Section 3 we saw through an example how the response time of a given task could significantly improve if we used the iterative best-case estimation, as opposed to the trivial bestcase estimation. In that example, the improvement in the response time was 25%. However, to better estimate the schedulability improvement we need to apply the best-case analysis techniques to more realistic examples, under different conditions. For our simulations we have modified a tool that implemented the previous worst-case analysis algorithm, WCRT [3], and we have adapted it to the new requirements of algorithm BWCRT. The modification of the tool just took us about one hour of work, which gives an idea of the simplicity of the new best-case analysis algorithms. We have also used the capability of this tool to generate task and message sets automatically, to increase the level of resource utilization until the system is no longer schedulable, and to perform an optimum assignment of priorities, according to the technique that we developed in [1].

We have carried out simulations for different relations between the best and worst-case execution times of the different actions, ∆=C b /C. Notice that a value of ∆=0 is equivalent to the old worst-case analysis, in which we considered the best-case execution and response times negligible. On the other side, a value of ∆=1 represents a task with a deterministic time, which is the case when the best-case analysis produces the best results. Another parameter that we found has a significant influence on the schedulability results is the ratio between the maximum and minimum periods for the external events, δ=T max /T min .

Figures 4 to 7 show the results obtained by the different simulation experiments on an example of a system architecture with 8 processors with 50 tasks executing in them, and three communications networks through which 43 periodic message sequences are transferred. The system responds to seven external periodic events, each with an end-to-end deadline that is proportional to its period, and takes into account the number of resources used by the different actions of the response (which averages to 10 resources). We have than if priorities are not changed, which shows that the priority optimization technique can take advantage of the best-case analysis. We can also see that with priority optimization the differences between the two best-case estimations are smaller than with fixed priorities, but they appear now also for lower values of δ.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper we have described an enhancement to an existing analysis technique based on RMA, for obtaining the worst-case response time in distributed hard real-time systems. The enhanced technique allows us to increase the maximum schedulable utilization of the resources, with a null cost from the application point of view, because the improvement affects only the analysis technique. This improvement is based on the estimation of a lower bound on the best-case response time of the different actions in the system, which allows us to reduce the negative effects cased by jitter.

We have proposed two methods for estimating a lower bound on the best-case response times: a trivial method, in which we don't take into account preemption by higher priority actions, and a more elaborate iterative method that is not exact but takes into account some of the preemption effects caused by higher priority actions. Both methods achieve good results. They allow increasing the schedulable resource limits by around 5% more utilization. The difference between the trivial and the iterative best-case estimation varies between zero and about 1% utilization.

div.p: chosen this example because it represents a relatively The first two graphs (Figure 4 and Figure 5) represent the schedulability limit obtained when the resource utilization is increased until the system becomes unschedulable. The limit is given in terms of the average resource utilization for all resources. In Figure 4 we can see the absolute increase in the schedulable utilization limits for the iterative best-case estimation, as a function of ∆, the ratio between the best and worst-case execution times. The schedulability limit is plotted for three different values of δ. We can see that, as expected, the improvement of the schedulability level is better for higher values of ∆, reaching almost 5% in some experiments. The improvement is slightly better for higher values of δ. Figure 5 shows a comparison of the increase in the schedulable utilization limits for both the trivial best-case estimation and the iterative best-case estimation, as a function of ∆. The experiment was done for a value of δ=100. We can see that we get a significant increase for values of ∆>0.4. The improvement is slightly better for the iterative best-case estimation than for the trivial best-case estimation (by an amount up to 1% utilization).
